Then the Imam called his servant Kafur: “Go and ask my sister Hakima Khatun to come here.” Her name means “the wise woman,” Sophia; a variant calls her Halima, “the gentle woman.” When she entered, the Imam said: “This is the young woman of whom I spoke to you.” Hakima embraced Narcissus tenderly. The Imam continued: “O daughter of the Messenger of God, take Narcissus home with you. It is through the testimony of this venerable woman, Hakima Khatun, sister of Imam Ali Naqi and aunt of the young husband, Imam Hasan Askari, that we learn the circumstances of the birth of the last Imam, the Imam who is yet to come. According to tradition, she related the following: “On the Thursday night of mid-Sha'ban, in the year 255 AH (3 August 868), I went to the house of my noble nephew, the Imam of the time, Hasan Askari.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01793

“When I was about to leave, His Lordship said: ‘Aunt, stay with us tonight. This very night the most noble child will be born, through whom God will bring the earth to life with knowledge, faith, and spiritual uprightness, after it has died through error and monstrous wrongdoing.’ I asked: ‘My lord, to whom will this child be born?’ ‘To Narcissus, of course!’ I looked at Narcissus, but I could see no sign whatever that she was expecting a child.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01794

“I was astonished. His Lordship the Imam smiled and said: ‘Aunt, when morning comes, the sign will become visible. It will be as it was with the mother of Moses, who showed no sign of her condition until the hour of birth, so that she might escape the measures decreed by Pharaoh, who was putting women in her condition to death.’”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01795

But this is not simply a matter of escaping Pharaoh—or the Abbasid caliph, who represents him well enough. Rather, escaping Pharaoh means escaping all the consequences that would follow from confusing the divine taking on human form in the person of the Imam with a material embodiment of the divine in flesh and in history. Every detail that the venerable Hakima is about to recount shows us how Shiite teaching about the Imams reproduces the essential features of a Gnostic understanding of Christ.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01796

What is at issue is a theophany, a manifestation of God—not an Incarnation, nor a hypostatic union that fuses two utterly different natures. The Imam as envisioned by Shiite consciousness therefore has features corresponding to a Christology other than the official one: the Christology which, from the Valentinian Gnostics to Master Valentin Weigel, would have regarded any conception other than a caro Christi spiritualis, the spiritual flesh of Christ, as blasphemous. One might call this docetism.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01797

But docetism, whether in Marcion or elsewhere, does not abolish the reality of the event. It does not reduce it to a myth or a ghostly appearance. It perceives the event on a spiritual level of reality where materialization and secularization—that is, reduction to what can be established through ordinary experience—are radically impossible. Precisely because they belong to a level beyond ordinary evidence, the features of such a vision appear as paradoxes. It is through these very features that Shiite teaching about the Imams reveals its Gnostic inspiration. Many illuminating comparisons could be drawn, but here we shall confine ourselves to presenting texts that have received little attention in the general history of religions.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01798

The venerable Hakima Khatun gives the following account in full: “Imam Hasan used to tell me: ‘We, the spiritual heirs (awsiya) of the Messenger of God, are carried by our mothers not in the womb but in the side. We come forth not from their womb but from the thigh, because we are the Lights of God Most High, and he has kept all stain and impurity far from us.’

“I went to Narcissus and spoke to her of these things. She said: ‘O Khatun, I feel no sign of anything within me.’

“Yet I decided to stay the whole night. I ate the evening meal and slept near Narcissus. Every hour I checked on her condition. While I watched her, the false dawn had appeared. I almost began to doubt that His Lordship the Imam would fulfill his promise within the time he had set. Suddenly, Imam Hasan called to me from his room: ‘Do not doubt, for the hour has come.’

“At that moment I noticed a certain restlessness in Narcissus. I took her in my arms and invoked the divine Name over her. The Imam called out: ‘Recite over her the sura beginning, “We sent it down on the Night of Destiny”’ (97:1 ff.). Then I asked Narcissus what she felt. ‘I think,’ she told me, ‘that the sign my lord foretold is beginning to appear.’ As I began reciting the sura We Sent It Down on the Night of Destiny, I heard the child within his mother reciting it with me and greeting me.

“I was frightened. Again the Imam called to me from his room: ‘Do not be amazed at the divine power that has enabled us to speak its wisdom and made us its witnesses and guarantors on earth.’ When the Imam finished speaking, Narcissus vanished from my sight. It was as though a veil had fallen between us. I ran to the Imam, crying out in distress. He said: ‘Aunt, go back. You will find Narcissus where she was.’

“When I returned, the veil had disappeared, and Narcissus shone with a light so brilliant that it dazzled my eyes. And there I saw His Lordship, the Sahib al-Amr—the Twelfth Imam, newly born through a supernatural birth.

“Facing the qibla, the direction of prayer, he was kneeling on the prayer rug, with both index fingers raised toward Heaven. Then he said: ‘O my God, be faithful to your promise to sustain me. Bring my office as Imam to its perfection, make my steps firm, and through me fill the earth with justice.’

“At that moment Imam Hasan called out to me: ‘Aunt, take the child in your arms and bring him to me.’ When I lifted him, I found that he was already circumcised, his umbilical cord severed, and his body perfectly clean and pure. “We shall bestow our favor upon those whom tyrants have oppressed on earth. We shall make them Imams of the religion. We shall make them the heirs. “I came to see him every forty days throughout the lifetime of Imam Hasan Askari, until the last days before his death. “‘He will succeed me when, very soon, I have left you. You must accept his word and obey his commands.’ Only a few days later, Imam Hasan departed for the holy world. And now, every morning and evening, I attend upon the Imam of this time. He instructs me in everything I ask. Sometimes he answers a question before I have even spoken it.”

Clearly, these last words of the venerable Hakima refer to certain privileged ways in which the Hidden Imam makes himself known, especially during the time of the Greater Occultation.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01814

But what we should notice first is the reference to the final days of Imam Hasan Askari, who died while still very young, barely twenty-eight years old, in 260/873–74. We owe the account of those final moments to Isma'il Nawbakhti; Nawbakhti is the name of one of the oldest Iranian Shiite families. This account is of the greatest importance to Shiite religious consciousness. Alongside the collected hadith in which, over approximately five years, Imam Hasan is shown presenting the child himself to an elite group of some forty Shiites, the account of the Eleventh Imam's death offers a twofold testimony: to the existence of the Twelfth Imam and to his investiture as successor.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01815

As his departure approached, Imam Hasan explicitly invested his young son, Imam Muhammad, as his successor. “Isma'il ibn Ali Nawbakhti related the following: I went to visit Imam Hasan during his final illness and took a seat beside him. He said to his servant Aqid: ‘Prepare me an infusion of mastic resin.’ Meanwhile the mother of the Sahib al-Zaman, the Master of the Time, brought the bowl and placed it in Hasan Askari's hands.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01816

“But when he tried to drink, his hand trembled so violently that the bowl struck his teeth. He put it aside and said to Aqid: ‘Go into the next room and bring me the Child who is praying there.’ ‘When I entered the room,’ Aqid said, ‘I saw the Child on his prayer rug, both index fingers raised toward Heaven. When I greeted him, he brought his prayer to a close and said to me: “Peace be upon you.” I said: “My master asks you to come to him.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01817

“Just then his mother came, took him by the hand, and led him to his father.’ The child's grace shone with light. His hair was curly, and a smile parted his lips. When the dying Imam fixed his eyes upon him, he wept and said: ‘You who are now to become the head of the Prophet's household, give me something to drink with your own hands, for I am about to return to my Protector.’

passage-en-01818

“The child took the bowl of mastic infusion (ab-e mastaki), moved his lips in an invocation, and gave it to his noble father. When Hasan had drunk, he said: ‘Prepare me for prayer.’ A towel was brought. The Child performed his father's ritual ablutions for him and anointed his head and feet. Then the dying Imam said: ‘O my noble Child! You are now the lord of this time. You are the Mahdi, the Guide, the Guarantor of God upon this earth.

“My child, my wasi, my spiritual heir, you are born of me. You are MHMD ibn Hasan. You are a child of the Messenger of God. You are the Seal, the last of the Immaculate Imams. The Messenger of God announced your coming to humankind. He spoke your name and your customary name (kunya). The promise made to my father and my forefathers has come down to me.’ With these words the Imam passed into Paradise.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01820

Such is the account of Isma'il Nawbakhti, now found in all Shiite works of theology and religious instruction. And it was very shortly after the death of his young father, Imam Hasan—perhaps within hours—that the child Imam also disappeared. We should not demand too much material detail here. The Shiite books say little, and on this point they can hardly do otherwise.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01821

For if entering the state of occultation (ghaybat) by its very nature removes all traces from the physical space of the material world, how could we search that world for traces of the transition? In fact, there are two occultations, or two degrees of occultation. The first is what Shiite theologians call the “Lesser Occultation” (ghaybat sughra). It began in the year of Imam Hasan's death (260/873–74) and lasted until 329/940–41.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01822
The second began at that very point. This is what Shiite theologians call the “Greater Occultation” (ghaybat kubra), and it continues to this day.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
en-book-7-ch-1-s3
3. The Seal of Muhammadan Walayat and His Occultation (Ghaybat)
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01823

The period of the Lesser Occultation thus began at about the time the Eleventh Imam, Hasan Askari, breathed his last. The child Imam vanished within his own home in Samarra, the house he inherited from his father, who had just died there. He disappeared into an underground chamber reached by a staircase of several steps. We seem to be presented here with an archetypal image. The chamber served as an oratory for the child Imam and his father. They were accustomed to retreat there for meditation and prayer, and also to escape intruders, especially the watchful agents of the Abbasid caliphate.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01824
We can easily calculate that the young Imam was five years old at the time of his disappearance, though some traditions give a slightly greater age.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01825

During the roughly seventy years of the Lesser Occultation, the Imam would be invisible not only to ordinary people but also to his own followers. He would nevertheless communicate with them through four successive na'ibs or wakils—deputies or authorized representatives. Shiite books preserve detailed accounts of their names and lives. The first was Uthman ibn Sa'id, who had already served as secretary and trusted associate to the Tenth and Eleventh Imams. He was succeeded by his own son, Abu Ja'far. Then came Abu'l-Qasim Husayn ibn Ruh Nawbakhti, and finally Abu'l-Hasan Ali al-Samarri.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01826

Through these intermediaries a number of Shiite figures, whose names are likewise preserved in tradition, were even brought into the presence of the Twelfth Imam. Apart from such occasions, the Imam appeared only sporadically: at his father's funeral and during the division of the inheritance, for example, to put an end to the unfounded claims of his uncle Ja'far, brother of Imam Hasan Askari. Other manifestations already resembled those that would occur in the time of the Greater Occultation, as we have heard in the testimony of the venerable Hakima.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01827

At the end of those seventy years came the momentous decision that inaugurated the Greater Occultation, which continues still. Here, above all, we can do no more than present the Shiite documents. The great theologian Ibn Babuyeh, Shaykh Saduq, whose authority we have already invoked, records what he was told in person by a witness involved in the events, a certain Abu Muhammad Hasan ibn Moktib. This man was in Baghdad in the very year, 329/940–41, when the Hidden Imam's last deputy, Abu'l-Hasan al-Samarri, died. He was visiting him a few days before his death when a sealed message suddenly arrived, sent by the Imam. He was allowed to make a copy. This was its content:
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01828

“In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. May God show your brothers his generosity in recompense for the ordeal your departure will bring them. Within six days you will meet death. Put your affairs in order. Do not appoint a successor to take your place as my wakil after your death, for the time of the Greater Occultation has now come. I shall no longer show myself to anyone, except when divine permission is given.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01829

“But that will not take place until a long time has passed. Hearts will become closed to compassion. The earth will be filled with tyranny and violence. Some among my Shiites will arise and claim to have seen me with their physical eyes. Beware! Anyone who claims to have seen me physically before the events of the end is a liar and an impostor. There is no help and no strength except in God, the Most High, the Exalted.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01830

Shaykh Saduq's informant completed his story: “Six days after that visit, when I had copied down the Imam's message, I went once more to Abu'l-Hasan Ali al-Samarri. I could see that his final hour was indeed approaching. One of the intimates gathered around him asked: ‘Who will be your wasi after you—that is, your successor, the new wakil of the Hidden Imam?’ He replied: ‘The matter now belongs to God alone. It is for him to bring it to its fulfillment.’ These,” adds the witness, “were the last words anyone heard him speak.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01831

But it is now that the secret history of the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, begins. What an extraordinary thing it is! In the starkest contrast to our obsession with the “material historicity” of facts, without which we can scarcely imagine that there might be “real facts” at all, the figure of the Twelfth Imam passes through history as lightly as a ray of light passes through stained glass.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01832

Yet for more than ten centuries he has dominated the whole of Shiite religious consciousness. Indeed, he is the very history of that consciousness, which for more than ten centuries has lived, in the secrecy of ardent devotion, in the company of the Twelfth Imam's mysterious person. The last words of his final message warned Shiite consciousness against adventures and impostures of every kind. That is why every attempt—and there have been several—to bring its end-time expectation of his coming to an end has been rejected, sometimes fiercely, as an intolerable blasphemy.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01833
Here, then, we must keep in mind all the distinguishing features of the Twelfth Imam that we have encountered throughout this work.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01834

Above all, we must recall the structure of Shiite teaching about the Imams and its sacred history: (1) the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of walayat, the latter being the cycle of the Imamate, or initiation into the spiritual meaning of divine revelations; (2) the double Seal of walayat: the Seal of universal walayat in the person of the First Imam, and the Seal of specifically Muhammadan walayat in the person of the Twelfth; (3) the perfect symmetry of the two cycles, in which each “Friend of God” in the cycle of walayat stands in relation to its Seal, the Twelfth Imam, just as each earlier nabi, or prophet, stands in relation to the Seal of prophecy; (4) the reasons why walayat, after the Seal of the prophets, corresponds to the simple prophetic vocation—that of a nabi who is not a messenger—in earlier periods of the cycle of prophecy; and (5) the reasons why Haydar Amoli opposed Ibn Arabi so firmly over the double Seal of walayat, and why his work has appeared to us as a great moment in “prophetic philosophy.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01835

For, as we have said, it is through the figure of the Twelfth Imam that Shiism intimates its deepest secret. This theme crowns the entire structure of its theology and theosophy. We have already noted the fundamental feature through which the theology of the Twelve Imams recalls the ancient Hellenistic and Zoroastrian theologies of the Aion, the eternal age. It is the idea of a twelvefold whole whose fullness has already been given, even though its final manifestation is still to come.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01836

For eleven of the Imams, the time of earthly appearance is over. Suspended in this way “between times,” the Twelver Imamate is therefore something other than what is called a “dogmatic teaching authority.” It would be a mistake simply to transfer to it the Western idea of a “religion of authority.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01837

Yet two things remain true. On the one hand, the Imams' enduring teaching, which reveals the hidden meanings of the Quran, is indeed the authoritative source. On the other, their persons, in their heavenly or metaphysical state, are themselves centers of Shiite devotion, because they are the Guides.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01838

This idea reaches its fullest expression in the notion of the personal Guide (see below, III, 4): the Imam who, though withdrawn from the sight of this world, remains present in the hearts of his followers, and whose supernatural invisibility protects them against any attempt to turn spiritual life into a social institution.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01839

The moving accounts of the Twelfth Imam's sacred life, and of the mystery of his two periods of “occultation,” are certainly not texts that can be subjected to historical criticism in the ordinary sense. That is why we have insisted that the phenomenological approach—an approach that seeks to understand a religious experience as it is lived—is the most fruitful for the scholar of religion.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01840

For more than ten centuries, the Twelfth Imam has lived a mysterious life in a region “which no mortal can approach,” a region whose coordinates cannot be marked on our maps. There he is surrounded by companions who, like him, remain hidden from our world. Many testimonies tell of occasions when he himself, or one of his companions, has appeared, but in such a way that those who encountered them generally understood what had happened only afterward.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01841

And these encounters are not reserved for exceptional people. They may happen to ordinary men and women whom great suffering, for instance, has shaken free of the certainties and comforts of everyday life. To understand such things, we need a conception of reality that has room for the “eighth clime,” the world beyond the seven regions of ordinary geography. An analysis that dismissed them as daydreams, imaginary inventions, or schizophrenic delusions would merely be confessing its own inability to understand them.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01842

Because the Twelfth Imam's time lies “between times,” the Imams who were his ancestors and predecessors lived in spiritual union with him. Together, the Twelve form a single Essence, given distinct existence in twelve persons. Everything that will happen at the end—the words the Twelfth Imam will speak, the deeds he will perform, the battles he will fight—is known to us through the Imams who preceded him. They themselves perceived these events through their sacred knowledge (hierognosis), a possibility fully accounted for in the theory of prophetic knowledge.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01843

One striking expression recurs in accounts of their visions of the last things: “It was as though I stood before the Resurrector” (ka-innî bi-Qâ'im ahl baytî; literally, “It was as though I stood with the member of my family who will be the Resurrector, the Qâ'im”), as though I were looking upon him. The same is true of the Prophet, who spoke on several occasions of the Imam yet to come.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01844

Thus the Prophet could speak of the day that God would prolong, if necessary, until the appearance of “the one who will fill the Earth with peace and justice, as it had been filled with violence and tyranny.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01845

For Shiite theosophical interpretation, the day that God prolongs until the appearance of the Resurrecting Imam (qiyâm al-Qâ'im) is precisely the time in which the Imam's followers are living now. It is the time of their own existence, the time “between times”: the Imam's occultation, the age of the Hidden Imam, who is therefore called sâhib al-zamân, the one who holds sway over this age. Haydar Âmolî explains it through an image. The cycle of prophecy that brings divine law began at sunrise with Adam and reached its noon with Mohammad. After Mohammad it was closed and passed out of sight, like the sun after setting.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01846

But the walâyat, the inner or esoteric prophecy that rose at the beginning of this night, began with 'Alî, the First Imam. It advanced from Imam to Imam like the moon traveling through the darkness, until dawn, rising with the twelfth and final Imam, would dispel the night. This night, then, is what we experience as “our time,” the time “between times,” the age in which the Imam remains hidden. It is the night of symbols, the night in which esoteric understanding is indispensable.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01847

We may therefore say that the mystery embodied in the person of the Twelfth Imam points to a secret of expectation: the waiting for the end of time that was already a feature of ancient Zoroastrian Iran. With Islam as a whole, this expectation accepts that the cycle of lawgiving prophecy is closed; yet it also affirms that something continues, and that something is still to come. We have already seen how the idea of a new cycle following the cycle of prophecy—a cycle of initiation into the hidden spiritual meaning of divine revelation, administered by the holy Imams—refuses to let religious life become fixed in a moment of the past, sealed forever.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01848

Shiite consciousness does not strain toward an indefinite future; it awaits an end of time, an eschatological fulfillment. That very expectation calls for a release from the merely literal reading of revelation, and from the imprisonment of its meaning in a past that literalism keeps closed. Conversely, no such expectation could exist without gnosis: some knowledge, or at least some intimation, of revelation's inward, hidden, anagogical meaning—that is, a meaning that carries the soul upward. This inward, upward-leading meaning, which holds the soul in a state of supreme expectation, is the very secret of the Imamate, of the complete spiritual assembly—the pleroma—of the Twelve.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01849

The coming of the Twelfth Imam brings the Integral Human Being, the Perfect Human (al-Insân al-kâmil), to completion. It reveals what other traditions of gnosis call the mystery of the Anthropos, the primordial or archetypal Human. This is why the doctrine of the Imams performs a role comparable to that of Christology in Christian theosophy.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01850

What other traditions call the pre-existent Logos is here called the Muhammadan Light (Nûr mohammadî), or the eternal Prophetic Reality (Haqîqat mohammadîya): the first creation, through which being is eternally summoned into existence by the imperative “Be!”—the Esto (KN) of the primordial Will that creates from itself. This Light has two intelligible “dimensions”: the outward one, revealed through prophecy, and the inward one, represented by the twelve Veils in which the Prophetic Light dwells during its descent and its ascent back to its origin.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01851

Together with the woman who is called “the mother of her father,” they constitute the complete spiritual assembly of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. With the twelfth of the Imams, the fourteenth member of this assembly, the Light reaches its full growth, and the mystery of its enthronement is fulfilled. Should we ask what would have happened if Islam as a whole had followed the teachings and doctrines of the Shiite Imams? What form would historical Islam then have taken? Perhaps the question is mistaken from the outset.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01852

For what we ordinarily call “historical” reality is only the outer shell, the ambiguous appearance, of a hidden sacred history whose events possess the reality and permanence of a mysterium liturgicum, a mystery enacted in sacred worship. That is why we have had to say that every attempt to explain Shiism solely through social or political causes, in terms of the laws of historical causation, misses the very essence of Shiite thought and consciousness.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01853

The time of the Imamate remains “between times.” This is not a question of political legitimacy or social utopia. It concerns the mystery of the Imamate itself, which began at the dawn of humanity with Seth, son of Adam, the first Imam of the first prophet, and will end with the appearance—the coming into presence—of the final Imam of the final prophet.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01854
We can then understand the passionate devotion that Shiite belief and practice center upon the Twelfth Imam, who for ten centuries has been the Hidden Imam, the Awaited Imam.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01855

The sacred biography recounted above tells us when and how this period of concealment began. More precisely, Shiite theologians distinguish two periods of occultation. The first began when the Eleventh Imam, Hasan 'Askarî, departed this world at Samarra at the age of twenty-eight (260/873–74). On that day, the child Imam, Mohammad al-Mahdî, also disappeared. His father had invested him with the Imamate in what was the last act of his earthly life, and it was as though Imam Hasan had taken the child of his soul away with him. This first period, called the Minor Occultation (ghaybat soghrâ), lasted seventy lunar years (until 329/940–41).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01856

During it the Imam remained unknown to the general public and communicated with the body of his followers only through four successive deputies, whose names we recalled earlier. A very small number of followers, however, were brought into his presence.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01857
The second period begins with the letter addressed to 'Alî al-Samarrî, whose text we translated earlier. This is the Great, or Major, Occultation (ghaybat kobrâ).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01858

Yet in this period, no more than in the first, does the Imam cross the threshold that irrevocably separates our world from the world beyond. His situation is like that of those who were taken from the visible world without passing through death: Enoch, Elijah, and Christ himself, according to the teaching of the Quran. Earlier we referred to the bodhisattva who refuses to enter nirvana until every being has been saved.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01859

The expectation focused upon the Twelfth Imam also has its counterparts in Mahayana Buddhism's expectation of Maitreya, the future Buddha; in Zoroastrianism's expectation of the Saoshyant; and in Christianity's expectation of Christ's Second Coming. There are also the hidden heroes of epic tradition: King Arthur in the Celtic epics, and Kay Khosraw in the Iranian epic.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01860

All these figures belong to the same family of heroes associated with the end of time. With their companions, they live mysterious lives upon an Earth close to ours, yet not our own. Here the mundus imaginalis—the imaginal world—is of decisive importance. To do justice to the phenomenon, the phenomenologist must embrace what we have called the “reality of the imaginal.” There can be no meaningful interpretation of the Great Occultation without acknowledging this world that exists alongside our own: a world containing all the forms of the sensory world, the world of mystical cities “where spirits take on bodies and bodies become spiritual,” as Mohsen Fayz so aptly defines it.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01861

A few privileged people enter this world and return, without any distinction of social class. Unless we allow for its existence, every attempted explanation risks destroying the very thing it seeks to explain. There have, of course, been naïve minds for whom the Imam must exist exactly like the people we meet every day. Some have even seriously discussed extraordinarily long-lived persons and the biological possibility of surviving for centuries.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01862

But let us remember that the last knights of Kay Khosraw also tried to seek him in this way. Where, then, were they actually looking? The Imam's invisible presence, his perpetual contemporaneity “between times,” means something else. It is neither a moral allegory nor a mythological representation. It is precisely the reality of that mundus imaginalis which Suhrawardî and the Platonists of Persia were compelled to affirm in their prophetic philosophy, because they knew that without such a world they could not account for the reality of spiritual, metaphysical, and supernatural events.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01863

Until the hour of his appearance, the Hidden Imam becomes visible only in dreams or in certain personal manifestations that have the character of visionary events. These do not interrupt the period of ghaybat, of occultation: they take place within this very time “between times” and do not become part of the stream of material historical events that any observer might record and verify. Shiite books contain numerous accounts of such theophanic visions, manifestations of the divine; they deserve a classification by type.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01864

Most often the Twelfth Imam appears as a very beautiful child or young man. He reveals himself to those in material distress or spiritual torment, perhaps at a bend in the road, or in a mosque where a believer stands alone. Usually it is only afterward that the person realizes the Imam was the one who appeared. Every Shiite believer knows that he may call upon the Imam for help. People even speak of the geography of the secret place where he dwells: the mysterious territory of the Green Island, for example (see below, II, 2). Later we shall note its curious—though purely nominal—resemblance to the name of the Strasbourg Knights Hospitaller's residence.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01865

But does not the Imam's last message also bear some resemblance to the last message of the “Friend of God” of the Oberland? (See below, III, 1.) Indeed, there is such certainty that life is not confined to the conditions of our visible material world that some traditions recount events from the Twelfth Imam's life in the invisible world. They even speak of his five sons, governors of mysterious cities (see below, II, 3).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01866

To meditate upon the invisible person of the Twelfth Imam is to enter the “Celestial Earth” of Hûrqalyâ, which bears so striking a resemblance to the Land of Light, the Terra lucida of Manichaeism. To “see the Imam in Hûrqalyâ,” as an eminent Shaykhî master put it, is to see him where he truly is: in a world that is both concrete and beyond the senses, perceived through the organ suited to a world of that kind—a world parallel to ours, yet different in nature.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01867

We can now understand the force with which Shiite consciousness rejects two errors that it regards as fatal. The first is the error of those incapable of theophanic perception, who blandly declare that the future Imam has not yet been born.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01868
Yet we have already seen why, through the spiritual significance of the number twelve, the Twelfth Imam must be both already here and not yet.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01869

The second, still graver, error is the skeptic's objection: the Imam was born, but he died while his father was still alive. For Shiite consciousness, assenting to such a claim would be like accepting an echo or anticipation of the declaration that “God is dead.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01870

The reason is that the Twelfth Imam embodies the same deep spiritual longings expressed in Christianity by the doctrine of the caro spiritualis Christi, the spiritual flesh of Christ. Such a being neither appears nor disappears according to the laws of biology and material history, the laws of physical birth and death. He is a supernatural being whose appearance to human beings—or withdrawal from their sight—depends upon human beings themselves. His appearance is the very sign of their renewal. That is the deepest meaning of the Shiite conception of ghaybat and of the Imam's return.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01871

As the shaykh to whom I referred a few lines ago explained to me (see also Book VI above, pp. 280 and 291), it is human beings who have imposed concealment upon the Imam: he is hidden because they have made themselves incapable of seeing him. He cannot manifest himself because he cannot be recognized. His coming into presence is not merely an event that will occur one fine day; it is something that takes place, day by day, within the consciousness of faithful Shiites.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01872

From this perspective, the distinction between those whom the traditions call the “companions of the Hidden Imam” and those they call his adversaries becomes strikingly clear. We also see the entire cycle of Initiation succeeding the cycle of Prophecy, carrying within its movement the mystical hierarchies that remain present among us, although unseen.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01873

To break this cycle of Initiation would therefore be to break the expectation of the end of time, and the reverse is equally true. We said earlier that Shiite consciousness could conceive of such a rupture only as an unbearable blasphemy.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01874

Let us recall once again the terms of the Imam's last letter to 'Alî al-Samarrî: “People will arise who claim to have seen me in the flesh. Beware! Anyone who claims to have seen me physically before the events of the end will be a liar and an impostor...” There is something graver still. According to a hadith reported by Mofaddal (Mofazzal), because the Imam is hidden, the entire esoteric hierarchy is also concealed, beginning with the Bâb (the “Threshold,” the rank nearest to the Imam).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01875

We have already had occasion to say this: not only anyone who claimed to be the Imam in person, but anyone who presented himself as the Imam's authorized representative (his Bâb), claiming personal investiture in order to preach publicly, would destroy the expectation essential to Shiite awareness of the end of time. By attempting to anticipate the Imam's coming, he would place himself, by that very fact, outside Shiism. Such a thing has happened, as we know: it was the tragedy of Babism, and then of the Bahá'í faith.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01876

But that gives no one the right to hold a school responsible for doctrines that negate its own teaching and that it experiences as blasphemy. None of this means that the Imam abandons his followers, however long the Great Occultation may last. They may see him not only in dreams, as we have said, but also in ways and circumstances more mysterious still.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01877
We shall now consider a few such cases, chosen from many others. First, however, we must set out three principles of interpretation that summarize what has gone before.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01878
To understand the accounts that follow, we must keep three things in mind—three things that followers of the Imam take for granted.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01879

First, the Imam lives in a mysterious place that does not belong to the space mapped by empirical geography. It has no coordinates on our maps. Yet this place “outside place” has a geography of its own (see below, II, 4).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01880

Second, life is not limited to the conditions of our visible material world and its familiar biological laws (the carbon cycle). Events occur in the Twelfth Imam's life during his Great Occultation. We have already mentioned his five sons, governors of mysterious cities that one of our accounts will allow us to visit. These sons have descendants of their own. Here we would do well to recall the way beings are engendered in Yima's paradise, in Êrân-Vêj.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01881

Third, we must grasp the exact meaning of the final lines of the Imam's last letter. Shiite theologians have always emphasized that the strict invisibility decreed and announced by the Imam is meant to discredit in advance every agitator or adventurer who might claim to be a nâ'ib, a deputy of the Imam, in order to legitimize a political ambition. Every such claim is, by its very nature, fraudulent.
